{"id": "2:133/q41", "question": "What levels of Islam and faith are described?", "turns_on": "Degrees of outward profession and inward surrender.", "positions": [{"id": "2:133/q41/p1", "position": "Outward Islam professes God's oneness and the Messenger, while faith adds inward guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Sadiq compares Islam to the sanctuary and faith to the Kaaba inside it; outward profession governs life, marriage and inheritance. Tabatabaʾi calls this a first level."}, {"id": "2:133/q41/p2", "position": "Deeper Islam is surrender with certainty and without inward objection.", "reasons": "Ali defines surrender as certainty; al-Sadiq says ritual acts with inward objection can still be association. Tabatabaʾi assigns this to a third level."}, {"id": "2:133/q41/p3", "position": "A fourth level is continual remembrance, choosing God's will and an illuminated heart.", "reasons": "Miʿraj and Haritha reports describe divine love, hidden knowledge, visions and eased judgment. Tabatabaʾi says each level has a matching subtler unbelief or association; he relates 50:35 and unimaginable reward."}]}
{"id": "2:133/q42", "question": "What does the verse imply about human acts?", "turns_on": "The relation of divine creation to human capacity.", "positions": [{"id": "2:133/q42/p1", "position": "Humans are compelled without choice.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports the Jabriyya's moved-branch analogy; Ibn ʿAtiyya says the verse refutes denial of acquisition."}, {"id": "2:133/q42/p2", "position": "Humans can bring their own acts into existence without compulsion.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports the Qadariyya position."}, {"id": "2:133/q42/p3", "position": "God creates capacity before the act, leaving a choice to do or omit it.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan attributes this to the Muʿtazila."}, {"id": "2:133/q42/p4", "position": "God creates capacity alongside the act, which the servant performs and acquires without compulsion.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan presents the Sunni view. Abu al-Hasan defines acquisition as relation to capacity; Baqillani locates the act's moral quality in created capacity; Isfarayini joins divine and created capacities."}]}
{"id": "2:133/q43", "question": "How is Jacob's question applied inwardly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:133/q43/p1", "position": "It applies to the Qaʾim from Muhammad's family, whose members ask children the same question at death.", "reasons": "Al-Baqir states the application; al-Safi explains it. Tabatabaʾi allows inner applications beyond the outward verse."}]}
{"id": "2:133/q44", "question": "What do earlier scriptures add to the argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:133/q44/p1", "position": "Elmalılı reads preserved scriptural promises as foretelling Muhammad, the culminating Ishmaelite prophet whom earlier communities had to follow.", "reasons": "He identifies Israel's 'brothers' with Ishmaelites; Habakkuk's Paran with Mecca; Isaiah's visitors and new praise with pilgrimage and talbiya; Torah's twelve princes with Muhammad's community. Greek Torah, Psalms, Gospel and Paraclete reports are cited, including Faraklit as intercessor or truth separator. Ibn ʿAbbas's Torah report promises two rewards; another names Mecca, Tayba, Syria and Hammādūn. He says Jews and Christians conceal or distort signs and links 2:40–41 and 2:121."}]}
{"id": "2:133/q45", "question": "What does the following verse's 'that community passed away' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:133/q45/p1", "position": "It refers to Abraham, Jacob and monotheistic descendants, a community now dead and separate.", "reasons": "Bursevi derives umma from an intended goal and followed group; 'passed away' evokes becoming empty."}]}
{"id": "2:133/q46", "question": "What spiritual rank has Jacob's family?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:133/q46/p1", "position": "They inherited a single monotheistic path as purified people near God, each with an assigned rank.", "reasons": "Qushayri states the inherited path and different shares of felicity."}]}
{"id": "2:133/q47", "question": "What indirect command is discussed beside the witness challenge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:133/q47/p1", "position": "'Do not let me see you here' forbids the presence causing the sight and conveys anger.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan explains the indirect expression."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q01", "question": "What does meeting mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q01/p1", "position": "Encountering or seeing someone face to face, nearby.", "reasons": "Al-Layth says it is facing another; al-Khalil defines proximity and encounter; Ibn al-Sikkit lists liqa, liqyan, liqya, and laqa. {"id": "2:14/q02", "question": "How is the form لقوا derived and pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q02/p1", "position": "It contracts from لقيوا by lightening or dropping the yāʾ and resolving adjacent silent letters.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash discusses deletion of plural wāw before the following lām; al-Nahhas, al-Wahidi, al-Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, and al-Samin give differing sequences of vowel transfer, yāʾ deletion, and temporary wāw vowel. Al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi contrast لاقوا, whose preceding fatḥa allows retention."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q03", "question": "How is لقوا read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted form and a same-sense variant differ in verbal stem and authority for recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q03/p1", "position": "The transmitted reading is لقوا.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi says recitation follows widespread transmission from the Prophet and Companions; a report in al-Thaʿlabi gives the same-sense laqu form."}, {"id": "2:14/q03/p2", "position": "A variant reads لاقوا, with the same meeting sense.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi trace it to لاقيوا and assign it to Muhammad b. al-Sumayfa; Ibn Atiyya also cites him, while al-Razi and al-Nasafi attribute the form to Abu Hanifa; al-Alusi mentions both."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q04", "question": "What is the function of إذا and the meeting clause?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q04/p1", "position": "إذا is a temporal conditional adverb, and قالوا is its response.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi says its answer governs it and notes spatial and surprise usages; Abu Hayyan contrasts temporal, spatial, and particle analyses; al-Samin makes قالوا its governor and parses الذين as the object and آمنا as quoted speech. Al-Nahhas discusses the relative clause and response."}, {"id": "2:14/q04/p2", "position": "إذا portrays their behavior as a repeated, enduring habit.", "reasons": "Al-Itqan compares the continuing force of the imperfect and cites 4:142."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q05", "question": "Who are the believers they meet?", "turns_on": "The notes vary between the Companions generally and Abu Bakr's circle.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q05/p1", "position": "The Prophet's Companions, including the Emigrants and Helpers.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls them Companions affirming Muhammad; Bursevi specifies the Muhajirun and Ansar."}, {"id": "2:14/q05/p2", "position": "Abu Bakr and his companions.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi and al-Wahidi report this identification."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q06", "question": "What did the hypocrites mean by آمنا?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb asserts legal status, inner sincerity, or an omitted object.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q06/p1", "position": "They falsely professed Islamic belief outwardly, including belief in Muhammad's revelation, without inward conviction.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari's Jewish reports specify profession before companions or the Prophet; al-Jishumi and Bursevi describe a protective show; Ibn Ashur says they spoke Islam's formula and favors legal-religious believer status without an omitted object; Abu Hayyan notes ambiguity between false inward faith and mere outward words."}, {"id": "2:14/q06/p2", "position": "They claim sincere inward faith, beyond an already known verbal profession.", "reasons": "Al-Razi argues that this claim reverses the inward denial they admit to their leaders; al-Alusi rejects the special distinction as unsupported."}, {"id": "2:14/q06/p3", "position": "The omitted object is what was previously specified: God and the Last Day, or whatever the believers believe.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says a Moses-only construal is remote; Ibn Ashur prefers taking the verb without any omitted object."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q07", "question": "Why did they profess faith to believers?", "turns_on": "The sources give protective, opportunistic, and derisive motives that can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q07/p1", "position": "To protect themselves and gain worldly benefits while hiding allegiance and obtaining information.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya, and Abu Hayyan name protection of life, property, and family; al-Razi adds secrets, charity, and spoils; Bursevi adds marriage and intelligence; al-Alusi says they fended believers off. Ibn Atiyya notes kinship clouded evidence and the Prophet feared a public accusation if he killed them."}, {"id": "2:14/q07/p2", "position": "To mock believers and Muhammad's Companions or ingratiate themselves with their leaders.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports these two proposed motives from Abu Ali; the mockery may include flattery of those they consider foolish."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q08", "question": "What does خلوا mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether khalaw denotes solitude, motion away, or mockery itself.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q08/p1", "position": "They were privately alone with their leaders.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi equates constructions with bi, ila and maʿa; al-Tabrisi gives the same sense; al-Raghib, cited by al-Alusi, roots khalw in an empty place, space, or time."}, {"id": "2:14/q08/p2", "position": "They went away, with

drew, or returned to their leaders.", "reasons": "Abu Malik says 'went away'; Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi cite al-Farazdaq's verse to explain the sense of turning or departure; al-Biqaʿi describes a private return. {"id": "2:14/q09", "question": "Why is خلوا followed by إلى?", "turns_on": "Whether إلى has its own directional force or stands in for مع or باء.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q09/p1", "position": "إلى keeps its endpoint sense: they turned or departed from believers toward their leaders.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari favors Kufan directionality because a preposition should retain its proper sense without proof; al-Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur explain movement, goal of need, or customary refuge. Ibn Ashur says this makes the Muslim encounter brief; al-Alusi notes an omitted first object. Al-Burhan favors embedding a sense of departure in خلوا, so إلى retains its directional force, parallel to لقوا."}, {"id": "2:14/q09/p2", "position": "إلى means مع, 'with,' through preposition substitution.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, al-Nadr, and others cite 3:52, 4:2, 2:187, 61:14, a proverb, and poetry; al-Tabari reports the analogy and other preposition shifts, with Yunus and a poet giving Arabic examples. Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, and al-Alusi call it weak or unsupported."}, {"id": "2:14/q09/p3", "position": "إلى substitutes for باء in 'being alone with.'", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says the view is weak and against al-Khalil and Sibawayh; al-Samin attributes permissive substitution to Kufans and Basran resistance; al-Alusi finds no proof."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q10", "question": "Why choose إلى rather than باء with خلوا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q10/p1", "position": "إلى clarifies a private approach or need; باء can also suggest mockery.", "reasons": "A Basran grammarian, al-Akhfash, Makkī, al-Jishumi, and Abu Hayyan describe the ambiguity; al-Mawardi calls the wording more eloquent and literal. Al-Alusi disputes that khalā bi explicitly means mocking."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q11", "question": "How is the hamza at خلوا إلى read?", "turns_on": "Hamza realization and vowel transfer.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q11/p1", "position": "The hamza is fully pronounced and the preceding wāw remains still.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi assigns this to other readers; Abu Hayyan calls it the majority practice."}, {"id": "2:14/q11/p2", "position": "The hamza is omitted and its vowel transferred to the wāw.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas calls this a Medinan softening; al-Tabrisi calls it Hijazi, and Abu Hayyan attributes it to Warsh."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q12", "question": "How is خلوا formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q12/p1", "position": "An earlier wāw becomes alif and is deleted before plural wāw.", "reasons": "Al-Samin derives خلووا and says the preceding fatḥa signals the deletion."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q13", "question": "What does shayṭān mean generally?", "turns_on": "The breadth of the word's application and the nature of jinn satan.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q13/p1", "position": "A rebellious, malicious being, human, jinn, or even animal.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi cites 37:65, two prophetic reports, and Abu al-Najm's playful verse; al-Wahidi cites 6:112; al-Jishumi reports Abu Ubayda; al-Qurtubi says distance from good encompasses the groups; Elmalili recounts Umar calling a prancing horse a satan; Ibn Ashur distinguishes literal fiery jinn from figurative human corrupters. Asad and Raghib add evil impulses of the soul. Al-Burhan says shayṭān generally means Iblīs, his followers, and his descendants; Ibn Faris, as reported by al-Itqan, says its normal reference is Iblīs and his hosts, while this verse uses it of humans."}, {"id": "2:14/q13/p2", "position": "A jinn satan also has an immaterial spiritual aspect and material evil forces.", "reasons": "Elmalili contrasts philosophers' solely immaterial account with Ahl al-Sunna's broader view."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q14", "question": "From what root and pattern is shayṭān derived?", "turns_on": "Root status of nūn, evidence from derived verbs and poetry, and possible borrowing.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q14/p1", "position": "From shatana, 'be far,' on fayʿāl with original nūn.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi says far from good or far along evil's way; al-Layth, Abu Ali and Ibn Atiyya cite Sibawayh's tashayṭana and Umayya's shāṭin, while Ibn al-Jawzi adds al-Nabigha's shaṭūn. Basrans and Ibn Ashur give distance from mercy or Paradise. Ibn Ashur objects that tashayṭana may be formed from the noun itself and not settle the root."}, {"id": "2:14/q14/p2", "position": "From shāṭa, 'burn' or 'perish,' on faʿlān with added nūn.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi prefers burning as naming Satan for an eventual state; al-Aʿsha's yushīṭ and the cited warrior poem attest perishing. The Kufans include failure or burning anger; Elmalili notes implications for declension; Ibn Ashur says derivation alone does not determine declension and cites tanwīn at 15:17."}, {"id": "2:14/q14/p3", "position": "It may be a fixed loanword from an earlier language.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur notes similar ancient terms and reported Persian sīṭān; Elmalili reports Persian div and a claimed development into Western dieu with opposite meaning."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q15", "question": "Who are 'their devils' in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the described private allies are human leaders, other associates, soothsayers, jinn, or inner impulses.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q15/p1", "position": "Human chiefs or leaders in disbelief or hypocrisy.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi, Qatada, Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas identify leaders; al-Jishumi prefers this as the majority, natural in context, and excluding soothsayers. Al-Razi says senior leaders can corrupt the land unlike juniors; Baydawi, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur distinguish senior and junior hypocrites. Elmalili says exegetes agree these are human satans and describes secret pacts; Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi say distance from faith can encompass named groups. Ibn Faris, as reported by al-Itqan, identifies their satans specifically as the hypocrites' human ringleaders."}, {"id": "2:14/q15/p2", "position": "Jewish leaders who urged denial, particularly Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf and others.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas traditions identify Jews urging opposition to the Messenger; al-Thaʿlabi and al-Jishumi give five names across Medina, Aslam, Juhayna, Asad and Syria, with name variants; Ibn Abi Hatim names Kaʿb and cites Abu al-ʿAliya, al-Suddi and al-Rabiʿ. Muqatil calls them Kaʿb and followers. Some treat them as soothsayers."}, {"id": "2:14/q15/p3", "position": "Polytheists or companions among polytheists and hypocrites.", "reasons": "Qatada and al-Rabiʿ name polytheists; Mujahid includes fellow hypocrites, while other reports include disbelieving associates or brothers."}, {"id": "2:14/q15/p4", "position": "Soothsayers, sometimes named and linked to their jinn companions.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak and others identify them as soothsayers; Bursevi lists five with differing names, and explains their supposed knowledge of secrets, cures, and divination by attendant satans. Al-Alusi says this explains the name, but al-Jishumi says context excludes them. Al-Burhan identifies the soothsayers as including Kaʿb al-Ashraf, Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab, and his brother Abū Yāsir."}, {"id": "2:14/q15/p5", "position": "Jinn satans themselves.", "reasons": "Reports from al-Kalbi and Ibn Abbas are cited; Ibn Atiyya finds it unlikely in context, al-Alusi implausible, and al-Jishumi prefers the human leaders."}, {"id": "2:14/q15/p6", "position": "Inner demons or a person's evil impulses.", "reasons": "Asad and Raghib allow Qur'anic shaytan for satanic impulses opposed to truth and morality; Study Quran lists inner demons as an interpretation here."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q16", "question": "How is شياطين formed and inflected?", "turns_on": "Broken plural inflection versus anomalous sound-plural treatment.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q16/p1", "position": "It is an inflected broken plural, with original nūn retained in annexation.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas gives genitive case after إلى and a genitive suffix. Al-Samin offers faʿālīl or faʿālīn patterns; al-Alusi confirms broken plural."}, {"id": "2:14/q16/p2", "position": "A rare anomalous plural treats it like a sound masculine plural: الشياطون.", "reasons": "Al-Samin compares the colloquial بساتون and cites 26:210; al-Alusi notes the anomalous reading."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q17", "question": "What does إنا معكم assert?", "turns_on": "Whether 'with' denotes religion, aid, intelligence sharing, or active harm.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q17/p1", "position": "They share their leaders' religion and remain in their faction.", "reasons": "Ibn Hisham, Ibn Abbas, al-Thaʿlabi, Damghani, al-Tabrisi, al-Nasafi and others read continuing religious allegiance. Damghani cites analogous use in 11:58 and 67:28; al-Alusi specifies Judaism and calls it a spiritual alliance."}, {"id": "2:14/q17/p2", "position": "They offer support or assistance against Muhammad and believers.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi, al-Jishumi, Ibn al-Jawzi, and Abu Hayyan offer support alongside or instead of shared religion."}, {"id": "2:14/q17/p3", "position": "They share intelligence about believers.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives this as one of four interpretations."}, {"id": "2:14/q17/p4", "position": "They join in harming Muslims and suppressing God's message.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan lists this as another interpretation."}]}

{"id": "2:14/q19", "question": "How is معكم read?", "turns_on": "Vocalization of the ʿayn.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q19/p1", "position": "The ʿayn is vowelled.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi call this the majority reading."}, {"id": "2:14/q19/p2", "position": "The ʿayn is still, an anomalous tribal form.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi assign it to Ghanm and Rabiʿa; al-Samin limits the still form to poetry."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q20", "question": "How is the plural mīm read near معكم إنما?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣila is made before the following hamza; other plural-mīm environments supply the comparative rule.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q20/p1", "position": "The plural mīm has ṣila before a following hamzat al-qaṭʿ in Warsh's route.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari lists معكم إنما; al-Hudhali gives Ibn Jammaz a generally no-ṣila route except this environment."}, {"id": "2:14/q20/p2", "position": "The other readers keep the mīm still in this environment and all readers still it at pause.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari also gives dialectal mīm and preceding hāʾ vowel rules elsewhere: Abu Amr kasras both; Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Asim and Abu Jaʿfar damma mīm; Hamza, Kisai and Khalaf damma both; Yaʿqub harmonizes. Ruways has two pause options in يَغْنِهِمُ الله; readers agree on damma after a dammated preceding letter."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q21", "question": "Why is their claim to believers verbal and their claim to leaders emphatic and nominal?", "turns_on": "How audience knowledge, intended reassurance, and social benefit motivate the differing clause forms.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q21/p1", "position": "They feign a new act of belief before believers but affirm stable allegiance to leaders, whose doubts need reassurance.", "reasons": "Al-Razi, Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Harali, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur explain the contrast. Hypocrites lack sincere belief and cannot convincingly claim perfect faith before perceptive Companions; Ibn Ashur says overemphasis itself would arouse suspicion. Al-Alusi prefers this account; the leaders might suspect genuine conversion after their careful Muslim-facing show. Al-Harali stresses their fixed allegiance. Al-Samarrai contrasts the verbal claim before believers with an emphatic nominal assurance of lasting factional allegiance; he also says the nominal form fits settled Judaism and disbelief that they gladly affirm and their own group accepts as genuine."}, {"id": "2:14/q21/p2", "position": "They assert strongly to leaders because they sincerely wish to reassure them, while they care little about believers.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this but finds it unpersuasive."}, {"id": "2:14/q21/p3", "position": "They avoid claiming perfect faith before perceptive believers, who would reject it, but their leaders accept emphatic reassurance.", "reasons": "Al-Razi, Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari develop this; al-Alusi reports and finds the stand-alone explanation unpersuasive."}, {"id": "2:14/q21/p4", "position": "Emphasis claims eligibility for Muslims' legal treatment and protection from conflict.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi notes they had already sworn by God and the Last Day to deceive believers, citing 63:1 as context."}, {"id": "2:14/q21/p5", "position": "They avoid calling themselves believers because their own beliefs give them no inward motive to say it sincerely.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai offers this as a possible reason for the wording of their claim to believers."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q22", "question": "What does إنما do in the last statement?", "turns_on": "Whether restriction belongs to the particle itself or to contextual interpretation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q22/p1", "position": "The added ما stops إن from governing, leaving نحن subject and مستهزئون predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi gives this analysis with a nearby مصلحون example; Abu Hayyan agrees on suspended government and says restriction arises from context, not the particle alone. He rejects deriving restriction from affirmative إن plus negative ما and denies attested governing إنما, citing 13:7, 18:110, and 79:45."}, {"id": "2:14/q22/p2", "position": "إنما restricts the hypocrites' claim: they are only mocking, not sincere believers.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says this emphatically reverses their public performance and confirms loyalty."}]}
{"id": "2:14/q23", "question": "How does the final clause connect to إنا معكم?", "turns_on": "Whether the last clause is a fresh answer, semantic reinforcement, or syntactic apposition.", "positions": [{"id": "2:14/q23/p1", "position": "It answers the leaders' implied objection: why appear friendly to believers?", "reasons": "Al-Razi, Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Alusi, Ibn Ashur and Elmalili describe this resumption. {"id": "2:16/q12", "question": "What legal inference is drawn from the exchange wording?", "turns_on": "Whether it supports agreement by conduct or limits an option.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q12/p1", "position": "Mutual conduct can conclude a sale without spoken offer and acceptance.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī describes taking an item and leaving its agreed price; Bursevī agrees."}, {"id": "2:16/q12/p2", "position": "A purchase option is barred for uneven units of one kind.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Mālik applying the metaphor to this ruling."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q13", "question": "How does the fāʾ link purchase to lack of profit?", "turns_on": "Immediate coordination versus an implied condition.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q13/p1", "position": "It coordinates failure with purchase and marks immediate consequence.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī attach it to the relative clause; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the act exposes both failure and lack of guidance."}, {"id": "2:16/q13/p2", "position": "It implies a condition: if they exchange, their trade fails.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī suggests this; al-Samīn reports a related conditional parse, opposed by Abū Ḥayyān."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q14", "question": "What does the negative mā do in فما ربحت?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q14/p1", "position": "With a past verb it negates the act without changing inflection, much like لم.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī contrasts nominal and imperfect uses, notes Ibn al-Ḥājib's contextual tenses and Sībawayh's emphatic mā, then cites 5:19 and a mā-plus-illā counting rule."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q15", "question": "What do profit and trade mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q15/p1", "position": "Profit is increase beyond capital, and trade seeks gain through dealing.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī cites a poem for tajara; al-Jishumī gives تجار as plural of تاجر. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr give commercial definitions."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q16", "question": "Why is profit attributed to trade rather than traders?", "turns_on": "Ordinary ellipsis versus attributional metaphor and its force.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q16/p1", "position": "Arabic attributes the trader's result to the trade; the traders gained nothing.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Akhfash, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj and later writers cite sleeping nights, resolved matters, 34:33, 47:21, 2:177, 12:82 and Jarīr. Al-Farrāʾ requires clear context. Al-Jurjānī argues this syntactic figure has force beyond literal paraphrase, with poems about drought and concrete idioms. Al-Akhfash also reports an alternative 2:171 comparison: gods and sheep alike do not hear or understand their caller. Ibn Qutayba says merchants are the ones who profit in trade, not trade itself. Al-Suyuti in al-Itqan classifies 'their trade did not profit' as a figurative expression at both ends, meaning that they did not profit from it."}, {"id": "2:16/q16/p2", "position": "Trade's causal or associative relation licenses figurative attribution.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī calls trade a cause; al-Zarkashī distinguishes lexical resemblance from rational association, citing verses on caused faith and ruin. Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Taftāzānī treat even the negation as figurative."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q17", "question": "Why does the verse continue the buying image with profit and trade?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q17/p1", "position": "The commercial words complete and reinforce the purchase metaphor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the end echoes the opening. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Zarkashī and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite poems extending images through nests, silk, birds and lizards. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes a literal companion from a second metaphor. Al-Baqillani calls the sequence of trading error for guidance and an unprofitable trade metaphorical. Al-Suyuti in al-Itqan calls it a reinforced metaphor, the strongest type, because profit and trade extend the buying image."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q18", "question": "What does their failure to profit imply about the exchange?", "turns_on": "Whether no surplus alone proves loss of capital.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q18/p1", "position": "They lost guidance as capital and all true gain.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī names confusion, blindness and fear now and punishment later; al-Ṭabrisī contrasts believers' trade. Al-Nasafī, al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr treat guidance, fitra or reason as capital. Sufyān al-Thawrī cites 61:10; worldly gains are no genuine profit."}, {"id": "2:16/q18/p2", "position": "The no-profit phrase alone denies only surplus; the next clause proves capital loss.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān replies to al-Zamakhsharī that a trader may break even. The second clause completes the thought, illustrated by Imruʾ al-Qays; al-Ālūsī says religious trade cannot end neutrally."}, {"id": "2:16/q18/p3", "position": "They gained nothing because they falsely expected reward.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān cites claims of divine favor and short punishment, then a hadith that Ibn Judʿān's generosity did not benefit him without prayer for forgiveness on Judgment."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q19", "question": "Is تجارتهم read in the singular or plural?", "turns_on": "Collective singular versus individual trades.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q19/p1", "position": "The majority read singular 'their trade'.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī notes weak transmission for variants; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī explain the collective sense."}, {"id": "2:16/q19/p2", "position": "Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla reads plural 'their trades'.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report that each person has a separate trade."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q20", "question": "How are تجارة and ضلالة pluralized?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q20/p1", "position": "Ibn Kaysān allows تجاير or تجائر and ضلايل or ضلائل.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives unhamzated forms and al-Qurṭubī hamzated ones; these are lexical plurals, not verse readings. Al-Zarkashi gives the wider rule for Arabic plural patterns: four broken patterns of paucity and the two sound plurals inherently indicate few, while other patterns can indicate few or many according to context, as Quranic examples show."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q21", "question": "What does 'they were not guided' mean?", "turns_on": "Faith generally, escape from error, purchase judgment, or divine knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q21/p1", "position": "They remained astray and could not escape misguidance.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn al-Jawzī explain escape from error; al-Baghawī offers general astray. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the past form implies entrenched, longstanding failure."}, {"id": "2:16/q21/p2", "position": "They made no sound choice in this purchase or trade.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī cite the purchase; al-Nasafī and Ibn ʿĀshūr portray ignorance of a profitable route. Ibn ʿĀshūr separates ordinary commercial discernment from religious guidance."}, {"id": "2:16/q21/p3", "position": "They missed the believers' profitable trade.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī report it; al-Ṭabrisī contrasts the companions and believers."}, {"id": "2:16/q21/p4", "position": "Their lack of guidance was already in God's knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya permits it; al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān report it."}, {"id": "2:16/q21/p5", "position": "They lacked knowledge of God.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports the explanation."}, {"id": "2:16/q21/p6", "position": "They forfeited the capacity to receive guidance.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān uses an absent road sign to illustrate missing means and distinguishes capacity surrendered from guidance attained; Bursevī describes invalidated innate readiness."}]}
{"id": "2:16/q22", "question": "Why deny both profit and guidance?", "turns_on": "Intensification, proof of capital loss, or distinct sense.", "positions": [{"id": "2:16/q22/p1", "position": "The pair intensifies blame: a trader may fail to profit yet act sensibly.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān make the distinction. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it also denies ordinary navigation to their aim."}, {"id": "2:16/q22/p3", "position": "The second denial attaches back to the earlier purchase.", "reasons": "Al-Sharīf prefers this; al-Ālūsī objects that the order and closeness of meanings weaken it."}]}
